summary:
MarsPath is a route planner for astronauts walking on Mars, built for Jezero Crater, where Perseverance is exploring. Pick a start, science stops and a destination, and MarsPath finds the route with the lowest modelled walking time over NASA elevation models, avoiding ground too steep or rough for a suited crew. Each route shows distance, time, slopes, a check against the spacesuit's EVA time budget, plain-language warnings and turn-by-turn directions.

It answers the challenge by layering data from several NASA missions in one map: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter terrain (HiRISE and CTX), CRISM minerals, THEMIS thermal imaging, the USGS geologic map, Perseverance's real stops, photos and MEDA weather, and DONKI space-weather alerts. It shows how far a crew can walk and still get back, plans rover drives with an Apollo-style walk-home check, and offers an AI assistant that answers only from cited NASA, USGS and science documents. Everything runs offline, as it would have to on Mars.

It matters because on Mars every minute of suit time counts. Tested against Perseverance's real drives, MarsPath's routes stayed a median of 61 m from the rover's track, against 122 m for a straight line.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

MarsPath is a route planner for astronauts walking on Mars, built for Jezero Crater, where NASA's Perseverance rover is exploring. A crew picks a start, any number of science stops and a destination. MarsPath finds the route with the lowest modelled walking time and shows:

• Distance, walking time out and back, steepest grade, total climb and roughness, each with a plain-language explanation.

• An EVA check: time out + time back + a reserve against the spacesuit's time budget, for the whole crew (crew size and carried kit are adjustable).

• Warnings, each with its rule, value, limit and data source: steep grade, rough ground, slow geologic units, lower-resolution terrain, suit-time budget, and recent solar particle activity.

• Turn-by-turn directions with heading, distance, time, climb and the geologic unit for each step, highlighted on the map.

• Three route profiles: fastest, gentlest (avoids steep slopes) and shortest, with automatic reordering of science stops.

• A walking-range map: where a crew can go and still get back within 25, 50, 75 and 100% of its suit time.

• A rover-assisted plan that checks Apollo's walk-back rule: at every point of the drive, could the crew walk home within their suit time if the rover failed? Rover speed and crew size come from NASA's Space Exploration Vehicle fact sheet.

• "What's here?" for any point: terrain, geology, whether it can be walked (and why not), and the nearest science site, rover stop and hazard.

• Real Perseverance photos and MEDA weather at each stop, a helmet-HUD view, and NASA DONKI space-weather alerts.

• An experimental boulder detector that finds rock shadows in 25 cm HiRISE images, for rocks too small for the elevation data.

• An AI science assistant that answers only from 21 cited NASA, USGS and open-access science documents, and checks every sentence against its sources.

HOW IT WORKS

• Terrain: USGS's Mars 2020 HiRISE elevation model (1 m) is the main surface, with the CTX model (20 m) filling gaps. Routes are planned on a 10 m grid built from these models. Slope and roughness come only from numerical elevation data, never from images.

• Route cost is modelled walking time: Tobler's hiking function on the signed grade (uphill and downhill differ), scaled to a suited walking speed, reduced for carried load, and slowed by rough ground and sandy or crater-rim geology (USGS SIM 3464 geologic map). Ground beyond the slope or roughness limits is excluded.

• An A* search finds the route in about 0.1-0.4 s.

• Seven kinds of data, mostly from NASA missions, are layered on one map: topographic (HiRISE, CTX, MOLA), optical (CTX imagery, rover photos), thermal (THEMIS), spectral (CRISM minerals), geologic (USGS), atmospheric (MEDA) and radiation (DONKI, Curiosity RAD reference).

BENEFITS

• Turns orbital and rover data into a plan a crew can act on: where to walk, how long it takes, what makes a stretch harder, and whether they can get back in time.

• Works fully offline from a packaged region, as it would have to on Mars, where every message to Earth faces a delay of many minutes.

• Every number has a source; missing data is shown as "not available", never as zero.

INTENDED IMPACT

MarsPath shows how future crews could plan Marswalks that reach science targets within their suit time. In one example, walking four science stops would keep a crew in their suits for 5 h 44 min, well over the 3 h usable budget; with a pressurized rover, the longest suit period drops to 40 min, and the walk-back check passes at every point of the drive. MarsPath also lets anyone explore Jezero Crater and Perseverance's real journey. We tested it against reality: routes planned between Perseverance's own stops stayed a median of 61 m from the rover's real track, against 122 m for a straight line, closer in 4 of 5 stretches.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

• Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML and CSS.

• Backend: FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pyproj and numba.

• Frontend: Leaflet (2D map) and Three.js (3D Mars globe), with no build step.

• AI assistant: hybrid keyword and local embedding search (BAAI bge-small-en-v1.5), with Google Gemini or Anthropic Claude for written answers.

• Hardware: runs on an ordinary laptop, with no GPU or internet needed once set up.

• Development: GitHub, pytest, and Claude Code as an AI coding assistant (declared in our AI-use statement).

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

• It applies Apollo's walk-back rule to Mars: the rover plan flags any stop the crew could not walk home from if the rover broke down.

• A helmet-HUD view over real Perseverance photos shows suit time left, the next stop, the grade ahead and the walk-home time.

• It is checked against a real rover's drives, not just designed in theory.

• An AI assistant that refuses to answer beyond its cited sources.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

• Astronaut limits: suit time with a reserve, carried load, uphill vs downhill walking, crews working in pairs.

• Honesty: MarsPath never calls terrain "safe". It reports modelled cost under stated assumptions, labels team assumptions, and lists its limitations: rocks smaller than about 1-2 m are not resolved by the elevation data, the data is historical, and weather is a past record, not a forecast.

• Mars-correct coordinates: planetocentric latitude, east-positive longitude on the Mars 2000 sphere.

• Communication delay: everything works offline.

• Usability: plain-language explanations, "?" help on every number, and a high-contrast design readable on a projector.
